issues.description: Specification silently widened: sign_message_by_id now always synthesizes the key, breaking signatures that previously used a non-synthetic path
issues.detail: The original DIDWallet.sign_message and NFTWallet.sign_message took the private key for the inner p2 puzzle and applied calculate_synthetic_secret_key inside the wallet method — that was the precondition. The new RPC code calls main_wallet.convert_secret_key_to_synthetic on a key obtained via wallet_state_manager.get_private_key(await did_wallet.current_p2_puzzle_hash()). For DID/NFT inner puzzles whose p2_puzzle_hash already corresponds to the synthetic key in the keystore, this applies the synthetic transform a second time. The postcondition 'signature verifies under the same public key the wallet previously returned' has not been demonstrated to hold; no invariant or proof was supplied that the two key-derivation paths are equivalent. TESTED-NOT-PROVED: the new test_sign_message_by_nft_id verifies that the signature self-verifies against response.pubkey, which it trivially will regardless of which key was used — it does not pin the pubkey to the pre-refactor value.

issues.description: signing_mode_enum is a non-total function over its declared domain — silent fallthrough to CHIP_0002
issues.detail: The free function signing_mode_enum in wallet_request_types.py enumerates three of the four (is_hex, safe_mode) combinations explicitly and returns CHIP_0002 by an unguarded fallthrough for the fourth (not is_hex and safe_mode). This is structured as an if/elif/elif with an unconditional return below — a smuggled goto disguised as an early-exit cascade. The author should have written this as a total function over the 2x2 truth table with an explicit final branch; relying on 'and the remaining case must be the default' is exactly the kind of reasoning failure that produces wrong code when a new SigningMode is added. State the precondition (is_hex, safe_mode booleans), state the postcondition (exactly one SigningMode per pair), and write the four-way case explicitly.

issues.description: Dead else branch in verify_signature: 'Unsupported signing mode' is unreachable
issues.detail: verify_signature in chia/wallet/util/signing.py enumerates the four members of SigningMode and then raises 'Unsupported signing mode' in an else. Because SigningMode is a closed enum and signing_mode_enum on VerifySignature has already coerced or raised, the else can never be entered. This is DEFENSIVE-AS-SUBSTITUTE: a guard pretending to be correctness. Either prove the case analysis is exhaustive (and remove the else, or replace with assert_never), or document the precondition under which the else fires. As written, the reader cannot tell whether the function is total over SigningMode or not, which is exactly the question this code exists to answer.

issues.description: Two parallel mode-dispatch ladders in the same module — invariant must be hand-maintained
issues.detail: sign_message and verify_signature in chia/wallet/util/signing.py each contain their own if/elif chain over SigningMode, with subtle asymmetries: sign_message branches on CHIP_0002_HEX_INPUT then the BLS_* modes then defaults to CHIP_0002 by fallthrough; verify_signature groups {CHIP_0002, CHIP_0002_P2_DELEGATED_CONDITIONS} together and raises on the default. A reader cannot verify by inspection that the two ladders agree on which byte string is signed/verified for each mode without simulating both in their head. The control flow is structured at the syntactic level but smuggles the correctness obligation into the reader. A single message_for_mode(mode, message) -> bytes function used by both sites would let the invariant ('sign and verify hash the same bytes for the same mode') be stated once.

issues.description: convert_secret_key_to_synthetic placed on Wallet is a category error
issues.detail: convert_secret_key_to_synthetic is a pure function of (PrivateKey, DEFAULT_HIDDEN_PUZZLE_HASH); it does not read or mutate Wallet state. Putting it on Wallet (and then invoking it as main_wallet.convert_secret_key_to_synthetic) misleads the reader into believing the synthesis depends on which wallet is calling it. It does not. This is the kind of accidental coupling that later causes 'why did we have to go through main_wallet here' questions and resists refactor. It belongs in chia/wallet/util/signing.py (or alongside calculate_synthetic_secret_key) as a free function.

issues.description: Test asserts the signature verifies against its own returned pubkey — proves nothing about correctness
issues.detail: test_sign_message_by_nft_id calls sign_message_by_id, then asserts AugSchemeMPL.verify(response.pubkey, expected_message_bytes, response.signature). This is tautological with respect to which key was used: any well-formed (pubkey, signature) pair produced by sign_message will satisfy it. The test does not pin the public key to the expected synthetic-of-inner-p2 key, does not cross-check against the pre-refactor implementation, and does not exercise verify_signature with address binding. TESTED-NOT-PROVED. To actually constrain behavior, derive the expected synthetic pubkey from the NFT's inner p2 puzzle hash in the test and assert response.pubkey equals it; and run the response through verify_signature with the NFT's p2 address to exercise the address-binding branch.

The new test calls rpc_client.verify_signature(...) but does not bind or assert on the return value. VerifySignatureResponse carries an isValid boolean and an optional error; an invalid signature would still return a response object, and the test would pass. The postcondition 'sign then verify yields isValid=True' must be stated as an assertion, not as the mere fact that the call did not raise.

issues.description: verify_signature docstring still references a 'request' parameter that no longer exists
issues.detail: The util's verify_signature was lifted from the RPC method but the docstring still reads ':param request:' even though the function now takes keyword arguments signing_mode/public_key/message/signature/address. Small, but symptomatic: the author moved the code without re-reasoning about the interface.

issues.description: Variable named hex_message holds non-hex bytes
issues.detail: In sign_message, the variable hex_message is assigned the UTF-8 encoding of the input in the BLS_MESSAGE_AUGMENTATION_UTF8_INPUT branch and a tree hash in the default branch. The name is a lie in three out of four cases. Rename to message_to_sign to match message_to_verify in verify_signature; consistent naming is a precondition for the reader's ability to reason about the pair.

DIDWallet's error was 'Invalid inner DID puzzle.' and is now 'Invalid DID inner puzzle.' A drive-by rewording in a refactor PR; harmless but indicates the author was editing prose rather than reasoning about the code.

review.summary: REFUSED as currently structured. The refactor's stated goal — extract signing into a library — is reasonable, but the author has not stated or preserved the specification. The original wallet sign_message methods derived the synthetic key from the inner p2 puzzle hash inside the wallet; the new RPC code applies convert_secret_key_to_synthetic at the call site to a key already retrieved by p2 puzzle hash, and no proof or test is offered that the resulting public key matches the pre-refactor public key. The mode-dispatch logic now exists in two parallel ladders plus a third unrelated copy in wallet_request_types.signing_mode_enum, the latter relying on unguarded fallthrough rather than an explicit four-case decomposition. The new tests are TESTED-NOT-PROVED: they verify a signature against its own returned pubkey, which is a tautology, and they discard the verify_signature return value. Before this merges: state the precondition/postcondition for sign-by-id and sign-by-address, prove (or at minimum test, by pinning the expected synthetic pubkey) that pubkeys are unchanged, rewrite signing_mode_enum as a total function over its 2x2 domain, and unify the message-to-bytes mapping so sign and verify cannot drift.
